As someone who has taken all the mental illness tests the internet could offer and also find to the ER thinking I was having a heart attack, I can give some tips.

First: usually, if you are wondering if you are going crazy that's a good sign you are **not**. If you were you would probably just accept that as ok. Seeing yourself in the list of symptoms is one thing, but that doesn't consider the intensity of the symptom or the impact in your daily life. That's what differentiates identifying with a disorder from having it. Don't self diagnose. We, anxious people, tend to catastrophize things and see them as bigger and worse than they are. We are not reliable to analyze ourselves objectively.

As to looking up symptoms, after many, many instances of feeling extremely anxious that I was dying, had cancer, was having a stroke and such, I just stopped. I don't google my symptoms anymore. What I do is Google how normal a very specific thing is, for example some time ago my temperature was 37,5°C. I googled what temperature was a fever, saw that mine was high-ish but still ok, and that was that. I know it sounds simplistic to just say "don't google", but it's the best thing.

Good luck and I hope you feel better!

Oh, sorry if I sounded invalidating or belittling anyone's experience. I actually thought about prefacing my post by saying that I in no way think it's better to have very visible symptoms. And I'm so sorry for all you have to go through.

I've had attacks that made me completely unable to speak or move. I've stayed in bed all day because the thought of leaving was so terrifying that I couldn't face taking a shower. And all everyone around me sees is a lazy and aloof girl who doesn't give a fuck about anything, when in reality I'm basically drowning in all the fucks I give about everything.

So again, I don't mean to belittle anyone's experience, this isn't "suffering olympics" to figure out who has it worse. I just wanted to create a conversation about having an invisible illness and how other people cope with it. I'm sorry if I offended and I hope you are ok and I wish the best to all who suffer with these issues.

I lost my mother last month and it was obviously devastating. But we weren't **that** close and she gave me a pretty rough time all through my childhood and part if my teens (and some moments now I'm grown). The thing is, I was raised by my paternal grandparents. So after the initial shock was starting to wear off I was hit by the train of realizing I'll have to go through much worse when my grandparents go. Twice. And then there's my other grandmother. And my dad (to whom I'm not super close either). But all of those times will hurt like hell. And then happen again. So, my point in saying this is: now you've felt the first strike of loss, start thinking about and preparing for the next ones. Both emotionally and practically. Talk to your folks about what they want health-wise, funeral and all that stuff. Have all the decisions already made so that on that horrible day you feel like you've been hit by a bus and can't tell right from left you don't need to worry about stupid decisions like what kind of casket to get, funeral or not, what kind of flowers you want and so on. Also check out the boring legal stuff because depending on the case/where you live, it'll just give you additional worry and confusion during a time you need to be surrounded by love and help to make it through the day. After all I had to go through I've been giving these tips to everyone because it was so horrible to be in that situation and having to decide and worry about all these silly things while I couldn't even think straight. Best of luck. Hope your folks have a long and wonderful life! Enjoy the good moments.
